title: ICESat-2 Mission Applications Program
abstract: Leadership of the applications program for NASA's Ice, Cloud, and land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2), from pre-launch coordination through the operational mission. The program engages prospective users — including through the Early Adopter program — so that laser altimetry data on ice, inland water, vegetation, wildfire fuels and other targets can be applied in decision-making, and evaluates the resulting impacts.
goals: Engage user communities with the mission before and after launch
Run the ICESat-2 Early Adopter program
Document and evaluate the applications and decision impacts of ICESat and ICESat-2 data
program: ICESat-2 Mission, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center
role: Applications Program Coordinator (2012–2015); Principal Investigator and Applications Team Lead (2015–2027)

issues: Abstract is an editorial synthesis of the CV grant entries and applications publications; PI to approve.
flagship questions/outcomes (2026-11-19): outcomes restate the linked publications' titles; questions are editorial — PI to approve.

questions: How can a laser-altimetry mission engage users before launch so that its data are applied quickly after it?
Which communities — from sea-ice and inland-water managers to the private sector — can use ICESat-2 elevations, and for which decisions?
How can the real-world impact of a science mission be documented and evaluated?

outcomes.text: Documented the applications identified through the ICESat-2 Early Adopter program.
Showed, through a review of the literature, that stakeholder engagement accelerated applications of ICESat-2 data compared with ICESat.
Applied the Science Impact Framework to real-world uses of ICESat and ICESat-2 data in decision-making.
Documented the value that ICESat-2 altimetry data bring to the private sector.

title: SMAP Mission Applications Program
abstract: Coordination of the pre-launch applications program for NASA's Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) mission, including assessment of soil-moisture data requirements across the prospective user community, an Early Adopter program, applications workshops and joint-mission tutorials with GPM, GRACE-FO, SWOT and ICESat-2.
goals: Identify the soil-moisture data requirements of potential SMAP users
Prepare users to apply SMAP data at launch
Develop the SMAP Mission Applications Plan
role: Applications Program Coordinator

issues: Collaborating organizations inferred from co-author affiliations in CV talk entries (pp.39, 37); PI to confirm.
flagship questions/outcomes (2026-11-19): outcomes restate the linked publications' titles; questions are editorial — PI to approve.

questions: What soil-moisture information do potential users need, and at what resolution and latency?
How can operational agencies be prepared to use SMAP data from the start of the mission?

outcomes.text: Set out the opportunities SMAP offered to applications users.
Assessed the soil-moisture data requirements of SMAP's potential user community.
Described how NASA science and engineering connect with Earth science applications.

title: Carbon Monitoring System Applications and Stakeholder Engagement
abstract: A sequence of NASA Carbon Monitoring System (CMS) projects linking carbon cycle science to policy and management decisions: engaging stakeholders, assessing data needs and gaps, and studying the socioeconomic value of CMS data products for user organizations, including scientist–stakeholder relationships and the program's community of practice.
goals: Link carbon cycle science to policy and management decisions
Assess stakeholder data needs, gaps and uses of CMS products
Evaluate the value and transfer effectiveness of CMS data products
role: Science Definition Team member and PI of applications activities (2011–2013); Principal Investigator, Phase 2b (2013–2015); Co-Investigator (2016–2019, PI: Jeff Masek, NASA GSFC); Institutional Investigator (2020–2022, PI: Vanessa Escobar, NOAA)

issues: Four separately funded CMS grants merged into one program record; PI to confirm presentation.
flagship questions/outcomes (2026-11-19): outcomes restate the linked publications' titles; questions are editorial — PI to approve.

questions: What carbon information do policy and land-management decision makers need?
What makes the transfer of carbon data products from scientists to stakeholders effective?

outcomes.text: Defined the capabilities and components of a terrestrial carbon monitoring system.
Showed that scientist–stakeholder relationships drive the effectiveness of carbon data product transfer.
Contributed to the synthesis of the Carbon Monitoring System's Phase 2 findings, gaps and recommended next steps.
Assessed the data needs, gaps and opportunities of the wet-carbon stakeholder community.

title: HIMALA: Climate Impacts on Glaciers, Snow and Hydrology in the Himalayan Region
abstract: A NASA Applied Sciences project with the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) and USAID to estimate the contribution of glacier and snow melt to streamflow in Himalayan river basins, integrating remote sensing and Earth system data products with an energy-balance snowmelt model in an open-source modeling framework.
goals: Estimate glacier- and snowmelt-driven streamflow in data-scarce Himalayan basins
Integrate remote sensing data with hydrological models
Transfer modeling capacity to regional partners
role: Principal Investigator (Co-PI: S. Habib, NASA Goddard)
methods: Remote sensing of snow and glaciers

issues: CV gives the grant amount as '$1.4 K' — likely a typo; amount is not displayed on the site.
Collaborators drawn from CV talk entries on pp.35–37 and 41.
flagship questions/outcomes (2026-11-19): outcomes restate the linked publications' titles; questions are editorial — PI to approve.

questions: How much do glacier and snow melt contribute to streamflow in Himalayan river basins?
Can remote sensing and Earth system data drive hydrological models where ground observations are scarce?

outcomes.text: Set out the HIMALA project on climate impacts on Himalayan glaciers, snow and hydrology.
Built an integrated system estimating glacier- and snowmelt-driven streamflow from remote sensing and Earth system data.
Integrated an energy-balance snowmelt model into an open-source modeling framework.
Applied and evaluated a snowmelt runoff model in an eastern Himalayan basin using Markov chain Monte Carlo data assimilation.

title: MERIAM: Modelling Early Risk Indicators to Anticipate Malnutrition
abstract: A project with Action Against Hunger, the University of Maryland and Johns Hopkins University to model early risk indicators of acute malnutrition, combining satellite-derived environmental data, food prices and conflict information so that humanitarian organizations can anticipate nutrition crises.
goals: Identify climate and conflict shocks associated with acute malnutrition
Build predictive models of malnutrition risk
Engage humanitarian actors in the use of predictive models
program: Action Against Hunger – University of Maryland – Johns Hopkins University
role: Investigator (28% effort over five years)

issues: CV does not state Brown's formal role title on MERIAM; shown as 'Investigator'.
Geography inferred from the associated Spatial Demography paper (Kenya, Nigeria, Uganda); PI to confirm.
flagship questions/outcomes (2026-11-19): outcomes restate the linked publications' titles; questions are editorial — PI to approve.

questions: How do climate and conflict shocks, together, shape the risk of acute malnutrition in children?
Can environmental and market indicators anticipate malnutrition early enough for humanitarian action?

outcomes.text: Synthesised the empirical evidence on climate and conflict shocks as factors in child malnutrition.
Argued for considering climate and conflict conditions together when designing interventions against child acute malnutrition.
Compared conflict and climate risk factors for acute malnutrition among children in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda.

title: Remote Sensing and Energy Balance Models for Scalable Agricultural Insurance in Sub-Saharan Africa
abstract: An interdisciplinary NASA project linking satellite remote sensing data and energy-balance (evapotranspiration) models to design scalable, more reliable weather index insurance for smallholder farmers in sub-Saharan Africa, including comparison of satellite evidence with farmer perception and recollection of bad years.
goals: Assess convergence of evidence among independent satellite products for index design
Compare satellite indices with farmer-reported losses
Support scalable agricultural insurance
funder: NASA Interdisciplinary Research in Earth Science (ROSES 2013 A32)
role: Principal Investigator
collaborators: International Research Institute for Climate and Society, Columbia University

issues: Collaborating organizations inferred from co-author affiliations in the 2014 AGU talk (p.32) and 2016 Reading talk (p.31); PI to confirm.
Brown et al. 2011 (Nature Geoscience) predates the grant and is shown as related work.
flagship questions/outcomes (2026-11-19): outcomes restate the linked publications' titles; questions are editorial — PI to approve.

questions: Do independent satellite products agree on bad seasons strongly enough to support insurance payouts?
How do satellite indices compare with farmers' own recollection of bad years?

outcomes.text: Used the convergence of evidence across satellite data sets for advanced weather index insurance design.
Compared farmer perception and recollection with remote sensing in an Ethiopian index insurance case study.

title: Earth Science for Famine Early Warning (FEWS NET)
abstract: Long-running collaboration with the US Agency for International Development's Famine Early Warning Systems Network, ensuring access to and effective use of real-time and projected vegetation index and rainfall data for Africa, Central America, Afghanistan and Haiti, and evaluating how remote sensing is used in food security early warning.
goals: Deliver real-time and projected vegetation and rainfall data to FEWS NET
Integrate food prices and NDVI projections for earlier warning
Evaluate the use of remote sensing in early warning assessments
role: Liaison and Principal Investigator (SSAI, 2002–2008); liaison and collaborator (NASA GSFC, 2008–2015)

issues: Programme-level record synthesised from the NASA and SSAI position descriptions; individual grants are listed separately.
flagship questions/outcomes (2026-11-19): outcomes restate the linked publications' titles; questions are editorial — PI to approve.

questions: Which satellite vegetation and rainfall observations best signal emerging food crises?
Can projections of vegetation conditions give earlier warning than observations alone?
How are remote sensing data actually used in food-security assessments?

outcomes.text: Developed intra-seasonal NDVI change projections for semi-arid Africa.
Reviewed the role of biophysical remote sensing and climate data in famine early warning systems.
Evaluated the use of remote sensing data in the Famine Early Warning Systems Network.
Developed country and regional staple food price indices for identifying food insecurity.

title: Enhancing USAID Famine and Malaria Early Warning with NASA Earth Science Results
abstract: A NASA Applied Sciences Decisions project with the USGS and Columbia University to bring NASA Earth science results into USAID's famine and malaria early warning systems. NASA ultimately combined the project with another funded effort.
funder: NASA Applied Sciences (Decisions CAN, NRA NNH04ZYO010C)
role: Principal Investigator; Co-PIs James Verdin (USGS) and Stephen Connor (Columbia University)

title: Precipitation Products for USAID Disaster Management Requirements
abstract: An internally competed NASA Rapid Prototyping Capability project examining precipitation products — including simulated Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) data — against USAID disaster management requirements.
role: Principal Investigator (with Compton J. Tucker as manager)

title: A Land Data Assimilation System for Famine Early Warning
abstract: A NASA Applied Sciences project led by the USGS to develop a land data assimilation system supporting famine early warning.
role: Co-Investigator (PI: J. Verdin, USGS; Co-I C. Peters-Lidard)

issues: Linking McNally et al. (2014) to this project is an editorial inference; PI to confirm.

title: Food Prices and Vegetation in West Africa
abstract: Two NASA-funded projects implementing interdisciplinary price models for Africa and testing whether satellite remote sensing can forecast cereal prices in West African markets, building on doctoral research on millet prices in Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger.
goals: Implement interdisciplinary price models for Africa
Forecast cereal prices in West Africa using satellite remote sensing
funder: NASA Applied Sciences; NASA Feasibility (ROSES 2008 A19)
role: Principal Investigator
collaborators: University of Maryland, Agricultural and Resource Economics

issues: Two grants ('Interdisciplinary Model Implementation for Prices in Africa', 2006–2009; 'Cereal price forecasting in West Africa using NASA Satellite Remote Sensing', 2009–2010) merged into one record.

title: Global Length of Growing Season Changes and Their Impact on Agriculture
abstract: A NASA Carbon Cycle and Ecosystems project analysing three decades of satellite vegetation data to quantify changes in the length of growing seasons and their impact on agriculture and food production.
role: Principal Investigator; Co-Is J. Tucker (NASA), K. de Beurs (Virginia Tech), M. Marshall (UCSB), C. Funk (USGS)

title: NASA Earth Science Data for Farmer Management and Agro-Input Mobile Systems (AGRA)
abstract: A NASA ACCESS project with the Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa (AGRA) and its partner ImageAD to put satellite information on vegetation, rainfall, temperature and soil moisture into the hands of farmers, traders and agribusinesses through a mobile website, mobile application and SMS text service.
goals: Deliver satellite-derived environmental information to farmers, traders and agribusinesses
Develop mobile web, app and SMS delivery systems
funder: NASA Advancing Collaborative Connections for Earth System Science (ACCESS, ROSES 2013 A36)
role: Principal Investigator
collaborators: Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa (AGRA)
methods: Satellite vegetation, rainfall, temperature and soil moisture products

issues: Description taken from the July 2014 AGRA presentation entry (CV p.33).

title: High-Resolution Carbon Monitoring and an MRV System for Ecosystem Markets
abstract: Two NASA carbon projects led by Ralph Dubayah (University of Maryland) on high-resolution carbon monitoring and modeling and a monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) system for ecosystem-market infrastructure, including analysis of the value of high-resolution forest canopy maps for Maryland's carbon sequestration and forestry programs.
funder: NASA Carbon Cycle Science (ROSES 2013 A5); NASA Carbon Monitoring System (ROSES 2014)
role: Co-Investigator (PI: Ralph Dubayah, University of Maryland)

issues: Maryland focus and Purdue collaboration from the 2015 AGU talk (p.32) and mentoring entry (p.55).

title: Understanding Multi-Scale Resilience Options for Climate-Vulnerable Africa (INFEWS)
abstract: An NSF Innovations at the Nexus of Food, Energy and Water Systems project, led by Johns Hopkins University, on multi-scale resilience options for climate-vulnerable regions of Africa. Brown contributed price and nutrition data sets and research on household electricity and child health in Ethiopia.
role: Co-Investigator (PI: Ben Zaitchik, Johns Hopkins University)

title: Geospatial, Farming Systems and Digital Tools Consortium for Sustainable Intensification
abstract: Part of the Feed the Future Innovation Lab for Collaborative Research on Sustainable Intensification, led by Kansas State University, building a new era of predictive agricultural innovation to improve the livelihoods of smallholder farmers through integrated geospatial, farming-systems and digital tools.
goals: Integrate agronomic, geospatial and socioeconomic models for sustainable intensification
Build decision dashboards for planning interventions
funder: USAID — Feed the Future Innovation Lab (SIIL)
role: Institutional PI (prime: Ignacio Ciampitti, Kansas State University)

issues: Collaborators beyond Kansas State inferred from co-authors of the 2023 Frontiers paper; PI to confirm.

title: Investment, Irrigated Rice, Dryland Agriculture and Afforestation in Senegal
abstract: A NASA Land-Cover and Land-Use Change project led at NASA Goddard examining the impact of investment on irrigated rice, dryland agriculture and afforestation in Senegal using SAR and optical time-series imagery in data-fusion approaches, including deep learning classification of regional croplands.
role: Institutional PI (PI: Christopher Neigh, NASA GSFC)
leadPI: Christopher Neigh (NASA Goddard Space Flight Center)

issues: Centre de Suivi Écologique from the Oct 2023 Dakar meeting entry (p.25); George Mason from co-author affiliations — PI to confirm.

title: Urban Expansion, Peri-Urban Agriculture, Food Security and Human Health
abstract: A NASA Interdisciplinary Science project led from Marshall Space Flight Center on the impact of urban expansion on peri-urban agriculture, hydrometeorology, food security and human health.
role: Co-Investigator (PI: Christopher Hain, NASA Marshall Space Flight Center)
leadPI: Christopher Hain (NASA Marshall Space Flight Center)

issues: Link to the 2026 Health & Place paper (urban spectrum, Kenya and Burkina Faso) is an editorial inference; collaborators inferred from the 2024 AGU talk co-authors (p.24). PI to confirm.

title: Satellite Observations and Models Informing Agriculture: Training for Open Science under Climate Change
abstract: A NASA Transform to Open Science (TOPS) training project led by the University of Montana, delivering open-science training on satellite observations and models for agriculture under climate change.
role: Co-Investigator (PI: Arthur Endsley, University of Montana)

issues: Geography inferred from the June 2024 NASA TOPS workshop in Algiers (p.24); PI to confirm.

title: Global Commission on Adaptation: Food Security and Livelihoods of Small-Scale Producers
abstract: Contribution as lead author of the food systems chapter (Chapter 2: Food Security and Livelihoods of Small-Scale Producers) of the Global Commission on Adaptation's 2019 report Adapt Now: A Global Call for Leadership on Climate Resilience.
funder: World Resources Institute and the German Government
role: Lead author, food systems chapter

issues: Grants section says 'Lead Author of the Food Systems Chapter'; the publications section (p.17) says 'Contributed to Chapter 2'. PI to confirm which description to use.

title: NASA Harvest — Food Security and Agriculture Consortium
abstract: Collaboration with NASA Harvest, NASA's food security and agriculture consortium, including a study of commercial agriculture's use of satellite remote sensing data for decision making.
role: Collaborator (no funding)

title: NASA Mission Data Latency Study
abstract: A study for NASA Headquarters on the data latency needs and requirements of users of NASA Earth observation data, and the societal benefit of low-latency data availability.
role: Study lead

title: Climate Fact Sheets for Zambia and Ethiopia
abstract: Development, under a USGS–UCSB grant from the Famine Early Warning Systems Network, of climate trend fact sheets for Zambia and Ethiopia examining sub-seasonal climate impacts on crops and pasture.
funder: USGS–UCSB grant from the Famine Early Warning Systems Network
role: Principal Investigator

title: Environmental Correlates of Food Security Risk Perception
abstract: A USDA Economic Research Service cooperative agreement examining environmental correlates of country-level drivers of food security risk perception in data from the Gallup project.
role: Principal Investigator

title: Science Community Familiarization and Engagement with Applications in the NASA Mission Life Cycle
abstract: A NASA Topical Workshops, Symposia and Conferences award supporting engagement of the science community with applications across the NASA mission life cycle, including the 2016 workshop on NASA data for time-sensitive applications.
funder: NASA Topical Workshops, Symposia and Conferences
role: Principal Investigator (Co-I: Vanessa Escobar, SSAI/NASA)

title: Pilot Application of the Chesapeake Bay Forecast System
abstract: A University of Maryland grant to serve as a pilot data user of the Chesapeake Bay Forecast System.
funder: University of Maryland — Chesapeake Bay Forecast System
role: Principal Investigator

title: Adapting to Climate Variability in the Senegal River Basin
abstract: An IGBP START PACOM small grant for African global change researchers, led by Aliou Dia at the University of Dakar, on adaptation to climate variability in the Senegal River basin.
funder: IGBP START PACOM (US NSF / US Climate Change Science Program)
role: Co-Principal Investigator (PI: Aliou Dia, University of Dakar)

issues: CV gives the award date (6/2007) but not an end date.

title: NASA International Sustainable Development Task
abstract: Task lead, for NASA's Disasters Applied Sciences focus area, of a group from SSAI and the University of Maryland's Earth System Science Interdisciplinary Center working on international sustainable development applications of NASA data.
funder: NASA Disasters Applied Sciences Focus Area
role: Task Lead

title: Inspiring the Eagles: Geography and Geospatial Science Capacity at Coppin State University
abstract: A NASA Education award, led by Coppin State University, to strengthen the university's capacity in geography and geospatial science applications.
role: Co-Investigator (PI: Douglas Reardon, Coppin State University)

title: Participatory Rural Appraisal and Remote Sensing in Senegal
abstract: Field research in Senegal on the use of Participatory Rural Appraisal reports as a primary data source, funded by the University of Maryland's Committee for the African Diaspora, which led to publications in World Development and Land Change Science in the Tropics.
funder: University of Maryland Committee for the African Diaspora
role: Grant recipient
